title: You are the Master
hookLine: too thaakur tum peh ardaas: You are the Master, to You this prayer; You are mother and father, we Your children

lines: A CHILD CALLS IN THE NIGHT.
cards: A small child wakes in the night and calls out one word. Not a speech, not an explanation: just the name of the person who will come.
The child doesn't wonder whether it's allowed, or whether the words are right, or whether the request is too small. It knows who to call.

Ashtpadi four has spent its stanzas on the forgetful one: you were fed, clothed, carried, and you forgot. Then, in the eighth and last stanza, the voice changes. The scolding stops, and a child calls out.

teach.h: THAAKUR: THE MASTER OF THE HOUSE.
teach.b: The stanza opens: too thaakur, tum peh ardaas.

You are the Master; to You, this prayer. Thaakur is an old word for a lord or master, the one a household depends on. Ardaas is the word Sikhs still use for their standing prayer, said at the close of a gathering.
So the first line names who God is, and says what's happening: asking.

teach.h: SOUL AND BODY, ALL YOUR TRUST.
teach.b: The next line, in plain words: soul and body are all Your capital, Your trust, held for a while. Then the line that gives today its carry: tum maat pitaa, ham baarik tere.

teach.h: MOTHER AND FATHER; WE, YOUR CHILDREN.
teach.b: You are mother and father; we are Your children.
Notice the order: mother comes first. Guru Arjan reaches for an everyday bond, parent and child, and uses it for the One beyond all forms. A Master can feel far away.
A mother is the one who comes when you call in the night. Next: in Your kindness are countless comforts.
And the stanza holds both: the One higher than the highest, whose limit nobody knows, and the One as near as a parent's hand. The forgetful guest of the last few days isn't thrown out.

The stanza ends with the guest finally speaking like a child at home. Guru Arjan closes ashtpadi four signing it Nanak, as the Gurus sign their hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib: Your servant, forever a sacrifice to You.

how: This stanza closes the fourth ashtpadi of Sukhmani Sahib; it is often said standing, just before the Ardas, and some say it quietly at night.

o: master or lord, the one a household relies on
a servant who keeps a great house running
a judge who settles a village's quarrels

games.q: the eighth stanza — tap the pairs.

s: ashtpadi four ends by throwing the forgetful guest out
it ends with the guest speaking like a child at home: You are mother and father.
in the line, mother comes before father
tum maat pitaa: mother, then father.
ardaas is still the name of the Sikh standing prayer
the same word opens this stanza: to You, this prayer.

games.q: after stanzas about forgetting the giver, what does the guest in ashtpadi four do?
o: argue that the gifts were earned.
call out like a child: You are mother and father.
games.why: the eighth stanza turns from scolding to asking: too thaakur, tum peh ardaas.

practice: Say the line once, slowly: tum maat pitaa, ham baarik tere, You are mother and father; we are Your children, as a prayer if you pray, or as a line of old poetry if you don't.
Then breathe in with mother and father, breathe out with we, the children, and let your shoulders drop, the way they do when someone you trust walks into the room.

wordCard.voice: Thaakur, master or lord: too thaakur, the opening of ashtpadi four's last stanza, where the forgetful guest finally calls out like a child.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: thaakur, master or lord, the one a household depends on; the stanza's first word for God.

carryVoice: Your line: mother and father. A good last line to hear yourself say before sleep. Rest well.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
